newsitem.title: NORWAY: FEATURE - Norway's Nera, a little known success.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Norway's Nera, a little known success.

text.p: Norway, known for its oil industry, fishing disputes and a stubborn refusal to join the European Union, does not readily spring to mind as a global leader in the telecommunications sector.

But the small Bergen-based company Nera ASA has become a heavyweight player in the niche markets for satellite communication and transmission systems, and wants to be a billion-dollar company by the turn of the century.

Nera is not a household name, but whether you want to use a creditcard to shop in southeast Asia, or make a phone call from the jungles of South America, it is probably Nera technology and equipment making it all possible.
The company started life in 1947 in the old Hanseatic port of Bergen on the west coast of Norway producing radio equipment and links, and systems for shipping communication.

Fifty years on it's a worldwide competitor in the telecommunications sector with sales amounting to 2.63 billion crowns ($403.4 million) in 1996 -- more than 80 percent of revenues coming from outside Norway.
Frode Botnevik, Nera's chairman, said the country's difficult and strange geography was largely responsible for the group's achievements.
"I think you can attribute a fair amount of our success to sitting in Norway, because of its rough, mountainous terrain, long coastline and its deep maritime traditions," Botnevik told Reuters.
"It was a very good environment for radio communication."
COMPANY AN INNOVATOR IN TELECOMMUNICATIONS

Nera's operations can be divided into telecommunications, data communications, electrical equipment and cables. But it is in telecommunications where it makes its mark as a world innovator with two main products -- microwave radiolink systems for telecommunications networks and maritime and land-based mobile satellite communications systems.

The group, which was listed on the Oslo Bourse in January 1995 after being demerged from the Swiss-Swedish electrical engineering giant ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG, has seen its order intake jump from 1.99 billion crowns in 1994 to three billion in 1996.

Analysts say Nera's competitive edge lies in two areas -- its international profile, due mainly to its close links with the maritime sector, and a good knowledge base at a reasonable price in the research and development (R&D) sector.

"Norway has a good reputation for engineers and Nera employs good, dedicated people," said an Oslo-based analyst. "We expect Nera to maintain a high growth rate, especially with its position in Asia. Asia has been the engine of Nera over the past few years."
Nera has spread itself far and wide -- its 2,000-strong workforce is employed from Latin America and Europe, to Russia, India and South Africa, and on to China, Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore.

Following its listing in Oslo, Nera was introduced five months later on New York's National Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation (NASDAQ) and intends to go public on the Singapore bourse -- the first Norwegian company to do so -- this year.
CUSTOMER PROXIMITY KEY TO BREAKING INTO NEW MARKETS
Nera expanded into Latin America in 1995 and last year began its drive into India and China. The company says proximity to the customer is a key factor to breaking into new markets.

"Our main strategy for growth abroad is to be seen as a local company and have local management. For example in Singapore, our main hub in Southeast Asia, there are no Norwegians employed," Botnevik said.

Analysts say Nera's future looks rosy at least in the near term with growth in the telecommunications industry likely to continue over the next few years from new investment from developing and emerging economies. There is also the prospect of deregulation in Europe and the United States.

Its most recent product, the WorldPhone -- the world's lightest portable satellite phone weighing just two kilogrammes (4.4 lb) -- notched up 3,000 orders by the end of January and had an agreement for potential delivery of at least another 5,000.
Nera remains ambitious. Botnevik said the company would focus development on the mobile satellite market and high capacity microwave generation to maintain its leading position.

"We will work on developing the next generation of wireless transmission systems. Today there are 2,000 telephone calls in one signal but the next generation will quadruple that, and it would be more sensible to have them travelling up into the air than to lay cables underground," he said.
"We want to be a global niche company. We have set a goal to be a billion-dollar company in 2000." ($ = 6.519 Norwegian Crowns)
